title: Boxing
sub: When a number suddenly ends up on the heap
cards/0/title: A number in an object variable
cards/0/body:
object is a reference type. If you put a number into it, .NET creates a "box" on the heap with a copy of the number and stores a reference to it in the variable. That's boxing.

Getting the number back out is unboxing.
cards/1/task: Step through and see where the box appears.
cards/1/steps/0/note: A plain number on the stack.
cards/1/steps/1/note: Boxing: a box with a copy of 42 appeared on the heap, and o holds a reference to it.
cards/1/steps/2/note: We change n. The box doesn't change: it has its own copy.
cards/1/steps/3/note: Unboxing: the copy from the box is back on the stack. m = 42.
cards/2/explain: The box got a copy of 42. Changing n after boxing doesn't touch it.
cards/3/explain: You can only unbox to the exact same type. The box holds an int, not a long. The right way: (long)(int)o.
cards/3/wrong/1: That would work for a plain int: (long)n. But unboxing requires the exact type.
cards/3/wrong/2: The compiler allows it: an object could be anything. The error happens at run time.
cards/4/body:
A number becomes an object when you put it where an object or an interface is expected:

IComparable c = 5;
old collections like ArrayList;
methods with an object parameter, such as Console.WriteLine("{0}", n).

Every boxing is a new object on the heap and more work for the garbage collector. Generic collections (List<int>) store numbers without boxes.
cards/4/deep: Boxing in a hot loop is a classic source of extra allocations, and it shows up in a profiler. String interpolation $"{n}" in C# 10+ goes through an interpolation handler with generic methods and usually avoids boxing.
cards/5/q: Where does boxing happen? Select all that apply.
cards/5/explain: object, an interface and ArrayList all expect a reference, so a box is needed. List<int> stores the int as is.
cards/6/q: Which line creates an object on the heap?
cards/6/explain: object c = b is boxing: a box appears on the heap. Unboxing on line 4 creates no new objects.
cards/7/q: Why is List<int> better than ArrayList for numbers?
cards/7/options/0: It stores int as is: no boxing and no casts
cards/7/explain: ArrayList stores object: every number is boxed on the way in and unboxed on the way out. The generic knows the exact type.
cards/8/pairs/0/1: A copy of the value moves to the heap
cards/8/pairs/1/1: The copy comes back from the box into a variable
